text: I'm in Arlington, Virginia, and this is an interview with Neville Kovach-Scott,
a U.S. Air Force retired. Where are you located?
You're talking about where I live?
Yes, ma'am.
I live in Silver Spring, Maryland.
Oh, right. Thank you.
But I work in Alexandria, Virginia.
Okay. And first question I'd like to ask you, when did you join the Army or the Army Air Force?
I'm here for February 20th, 1942.
All right. When did you retire?
I retired September 1968.
All right. During that time, what were your primary responsibilities?
Well, mostly flight nursing.
First, we went out as the first group of flight nurses, without any training,
to the South Pacific and the evacuation stations.
from the White Canal area back to Houston,
and then get in the Black Islands,
and get to Caledonia, the Hebrides, and so on.
And then after that, I came back to the States
and taught flight nursing.
And we had three tours in the Pacific as flight nurses.
And then I taught at Gensher, I taught flight nursing,
Then I came to the headquarters as an assignment nurse for all nurses in the Air Force.
Then went back overseas again to Japan for three years and came back as Chief of the Air Force Nurse Corps for five years.
Then I retired.
Alright, so you were Chief of the Air Force Nurse Corps for what year?
Um, 63 to 67.
Alright, and do you remember the...
For 68, 68, 64, that was five years.
Okay, and when you retired, do you remember the strength, roughly the strength of the Air Force first?
I think it was about 2,500 to 3,000.
And would that, when you first joined the New York Air Force, over the years, was that the high number of 3,000 or was that?
Well, the Air Force separated the Army, of course, and became the Air Force in 1949.
And at that time the Army let the Air Force have 1,199 nurses that could come to transfer the Air Force.
And so that's where we started with 1,199.
And then during the career war and all that we grew and I think the highest was, you know,
just under 3,000 I believe.
That's the best of my memory.
So your career was about roughly 30 years?
Twenty-six and a half, 27 years.
So during that time you got to know about so many nurses?
Oh yes, in assignments I learned everyone's names really.
I was in assignments for about three years, and I learned every one of the 15s.
About what year was that?
Oh, that was in 54 to 58.
I see.
Okay, then during this period, when did you become acquainted with Lucille Slatt?
Well, I ran into her all along for several years.
She was a peer, as both of us joined about the same time.
and she was a chief nurse in one place and I might have been assigned to another place.
But I was in contact with her off and on at meetings and different other things for several years.
So I don't know if I can put you on tape, but even before I knew her, I heard about her, you know, because she was a capable person.
Okay.
Okay?
All right. Did Bluefield's Lottery have any of your know-by-names?
What's the most common thing patients call?
The only one I can think of now is slats.
We all sort of call her slats.
Either slattery or slats.
But to shorten the name, it's slats.
Did you know any other nurses that were called slats?
Not that I can recall at all, no.
I think that's probably my final question.
I'll turn this machine off.
Okay.
